module_title: Sizing and Siting a Water Tank

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Demand Assessment and Daily Water Budgeting for African Households and Businesses
lessons.body: Before you buy a single bag of cement or a plastic tank, you must know exactly how much water you need. This is the foundation of every profitable tank project. In Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, and Ghana, water scarcity is not just a rural problem; urban businesses lose money when tanks are undersized. A hotel in Kisumu with 20 rooms needs 4,000 litres per day just for guests, while a small poultry farm in Ogun State with 500 birds needs 150 litres daily for drinking and cleaning. Your job as a tank constructor is to calculate demand accurately, then add a buffer. Start with a simple water audit. List every use: drinking, cooking, bathing, laundry, toilet flushing, livestock, irrigation, car washing, and construction. Use standard figures: a person in a Kenyan household uses 20 litres per day for basic needs, but in a middle-income home with flush toilets and a shower, that jumps to 80-120 litres. A restaurant in Accra uses 15 litres per customer per day. A primary school with 300 pupils needs 1,500 litres per day if there are no flush toilets, and 4,500 litres if there are. For livestock, a dairy cow in South Africa drinks 60-100 litres daily, a goat 5 litres, and a chicken 0.3 litres. Irrigation for a 0.5-hectare vegetable plot in Ghana requires 20,000 litres per week during dry season. Once you have the daily total, multiply by the number of days of autonomy you want. In most African contexts, aim for 3 to 7 days of storage. Why? Because boreholes break down, municipal supplies in Lagos or Nairobi can be intermittent for days, and rainy seasons can delay refilling. A family of six in a middle-income Nairobi estate using 100 litres per person per day needs 600 litres daily. For 5 days autonomy, that is 3,000 litres. Add 20% for future growth and evaporation, and you need a 3,600-litre tank. Round up to 4,000 litres. For a small hotel in Mombasa with 20 rooms and 2 guests per room, each using 150 litres per day, demand is 6,000 litres daily. For 3 days autonomy, 18,000 litres, plus 20% buffer equals 21,600 litres. You would recommend two 10,000-litre tanks or one 20,000-litre tank. Costs: in Kenya, a 10,000-litre plastic tank from Elgon or Kentainers costs KES 85,000 to KES 120,000. A 20,000-litre tank costs KES 180,000 to KES 250,000. In Nigeria, a 10,000-litre plastic tank from GeePee or Dangote costs NGN 450,000 to NGN 600,000. In Ghana, a 10,000-litre tank from Duraplast costs GHS 4,500 to GHS 6,000. In South Africa, a 10,000-litre JoJo tank costs ZAR 18,000 to ZAR 25,000. These are real numbers as of 2024, but prices fluctuate with exchange rates and transport. Always quote a range and add 10% for delivery. For ferrocement and concrete tanks, you can build larger capacities cheaper per litre. A 20,000-litre ferrocement tank in Kenya costs about KES 150,000 in materials and labour, versus KES 200,000 for plastic. But plastic is faster to install and easier to move. Your demand assessment must also consider peak flow. A tank that is too small will empty in hours during a party or harvest season. A tank that is too large wastes money and space. Use a simple formula: Tank capacity = (Daily demand x Days of autonomy) + 20% buffer. Write this down and show the client. They will trust you more. Also consider water quality. If you are storing rainwater, you need a first-flush diverter and a filter. If you are storing borehole water with iron or manganese, you need aeration and settling before storage. These affect tank design. For example, a ferrocement tank with a sloped floor and drain valve is better for high-sediment water than a plastic tank with a flat bottom. Finally, document everything. Create a one-page water budget table for each client. Include daily use, days of autonomy, buffer, and recommended tank size. This becomes your sales tool. In Africa, word-of-mouth is powerful. A well-sized tank that never runs dry will get you five more clients. A tank that overflows or runs dry in two days will get you none. So take the time to measure, ask questions, and calculate. Your reputation depends on it.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Site Selection, Foundation Design, and Soil Considerations for African Terrain
lessons.body: Where you put a tank is as important as how big it is. A poorly sited tank can crack, sink, or contaminate water. In Africa, we deal with expansive clay soils in Nigeria, sandy soils in coastal Kenya, rocky ground in Ghana, and steep slopes in South Africa. Each requires a different approach. Start with access. The tank must be reachable by delivery trucks, maintenance teams, and the user. A 10,000-litre plastic tank is 2.2 metres in diameter and 2.5 metres tall. It needs a flat area at least 3 metres by 3 metres. A 20,000-litre ferrocement tank can be 4 metres in diameter and 2 metres tall, needing a 5-metre by 5-metre pad. If the site is on a slope, you must cut and fill to create a level platform. Never place a tank on uncompacted fill. It will settle and crack. For plastic tanks, the manufacturer requires a reinforced concrete pad at least 100mm thick with wire mesh. For ferrocement and concrete tanks, you need a ring beam or a full slab. In Kenya, a 100mm thick concrete pad with BRRC mesh for a 10,000-litre tank costs about KES 25,000 in materials and labour. In Nigeria, a similar pad costs NGN 120,000. In Ghana, GHS 1,200. In South Africa, ZAR 4,500. These costs are for a 3m x 3m pad. If the soil is expansive clay, you must excavate 300mm deep, replace with compacted murram or hardcore, then pour a 150mm slab with two layers of mesh. This doubles the cost but prevents cracking. If the soil is sandy, you need a wider footing to spread the load. A 10,000-litre tank full of water weighs 10 tonnes. That is 10,000 kg on a 3m x 3m area, which is 1,111 kg per square metre. Sandy soil can bear 50-100 kPa, which is 5,000-10,000 kg per square metre, so it is fine if the pad is wide enough. But if the sand is loose, you must compact it or use a geotextile membrane. In coastal Mombasa or Lagos, the water table is high. You cannot dig deep. Use a raised pad 300mm above ground and build a berm. For rocky ground, you may need to chip or blast. In Ghana, a site with laterite rock requires a jackhammer. Budget extra for labour. Now consider drainage. The tank area must be graded so that rainwater flows away from the foundation. If water pools around the base, it will seep under and cause settlement. Dig a French drain or a shallow channel. In heavy rain areas like the Niger Delta or western Kenya, add a 300mm high concrete kerb around the pad. Also consider the sun. In hot areas like northern Nigeria or the Sahel, plastic tanks degrade under UV light. They become brittle and crack. Either shade the tank with a roof or use a black UV-stabilised tank. Ferrocement and concrete tanks are not affected by UV, but they can grow algae if exposed to sunlight. Paint them with white or light-coloured lime wash to reflect heat and reduce algae. For brick tanks, the mortar must be protected from direct sun to prevent cracking. Site the tank away from trees. Roots can lift the foundation, and leaves can clog gutters. In South Africa, a JoJo tank under a wattle tree will have roots in the pad within two years. Keep at least 5 metres from large trees. Also keep away from septic tanks, pit latrines, and animal pens. A tank 10 metres downslope from a latrine can draw contaminated water. The World Health Organization recommends at least 30 metres between a water tank and a latrine, and the tank should be uphill. If you cannot achieve that, seal the tank and use a hand pump or a piped outlet. For security, place the tank where you can see it. In urban areas of Nairobi or Johannesburg, a tank in a dark corner can be vandalised or stolen. A 10,000-litre plastic tank is a valuable item. Build a lockable tap or a cage. Finally, think about future expansion. Leave space for a second tank. Many clients start with 5,000 litres and later add another 5,000. If you site the first tank in the middle of the yard, you block yourself. Put it in a corner and leave room. Document the site with photos and a simple sketch. Note the soil type, slope, water table, and distance to water source. This becomes your construction plan. A good site saves you money on foundation and prevents callbacks. A bad site costs you twice.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Material Selection and Cost Comparison for Ferrocement, Concrete, Plastic, and Brick Tanks
lessons.body: Choosing the right material for a water tank in Africa is a business decision. You must balance cost, durability, local availability, and labour skills. Let us compare four common types: plastic, ferrocement, concrete, and brick. We will use a 10,000-litre tank as the benchmark. Plastic tanks are the most popular for small to medium capacities. In Kenya, a 10,000-litre tank from Kentainers or Elgon costs KES 85,000 to KES 120,000. In Nigeria, GeePee or Dangote costs NGN 450,000 to NGN 600,000. In Ghana, Duraplast costs GHS 4,500 to GHS 6,000. In South Africa, JoJo costs ZAR 18,000 to ZAR 25,000. These tanks are ready in one day. You just need a pad. They are food-grade, UV-stabilised, and easy to clean. But they can crack if dropped, and they are not repairable easily. A crack in a plastic tank means a new tank. Also, they are not suitable for very large capacities above 20,000 litres because the walls bulge. You can buy a 20,000-litre plastic tank, but it costs almost twice as much per litre as a 10,000-litre one. Ferrocement tanks are built on site using wire mesh, cement, sand, and a waterproof coating. They are excellent for 5,000 to 100,000 litres. In Kenya, a 10,000-litre ferrocement tank costs about KES 70,000 to KES 90,000 in materials and labour. In Nigeria, NGN 350,000 to NGN 450,000. In Ghana, GHS 3,500 to GHS 4,500. In South Africa, ZAR 15,000 to ZAR 20,000. Ferrocement is labour-intensive but uses local skills. It can be built in remote areas where trucks cannot reach. It is repairable: you can patch cracks with mortar. It has a long life, 20-30 years if maintained. But it requires a skilled artisan. A bad ferrocement tank will leak within a year. You need a good mix: 1 part cement to 2 parts sand, with chicken wire and BRRC mesh. The wall thickness is 25-40mm. You must cure it for 7 days, keeping it wet. Then apply a waterproof coating like Sika or a cement-based slurry. Concrete tanks are similar to ferrocement but use steel rebar and thicker walls, 100-150mm. They are stronger and better for underground or partially buried tanks. A 10,000-litre concrete tank in Kenya costs KES 100,000 to KES 130,000. In Nigeria, NGN 500,000 to NGN 650,000. In Ghana, GHS 5,000 to GHS 6,500. In South Africa, ZAR 22,000 to ZAR 28,000. Concrete is durable, 50+ years, and can be built in any shape. But it is heavy, requires formwork, and needs a strong foundation. It also cracks if not reinforced properly. You must use at least 8mm rebar at 200mm centres, and a 1:2:3 mix. Curing is critical: 14 days. Brick tanks are common in Ghana and Nigeria. They use burnt bricks or concrete blocks, plastered with cement mortar. A 10,000-litre brick tank costs about GHS 3,000 to GHS 4,000 in Ghana, and NGN 300,000 to NGN 400,000 in Nigeria. In Kenya, KES 60,000 to KES 80,000. Bricks are cheap and local. But they are porous. You must plaster both inside and outside with a rich mix, 1:3, and add a waterproofing agent. Without it, you lose water. Brick tanks are also prone to cracking from thermal movement. They are best for underground or shaded locations. Now, compare cost per litre. Plastic: KES 8.5 to 12 per litre. Ferrocement: KES 7 to 9 per litre. Concrete: KES 10 to 13 per litre. Brick: KES 6 to 8 per litre. So brick and ferrocement are cheapest per litre, but they require more labour and skill. Plastic is fastest and most convenient. Your choice depends on the client. A busy hotel in Nairobi wants a plastic tank installed tomorrow. A rural school in Tanzania with a donor budget wants a ferrocement tank that can be built by local masons. A homeowner in Lagos with a small yard wants a brick tank underground. Always quote both options. Show the client the trade-off: plastic is 30% more expensive but saves 5 days of labour. Ferrocement is cheaper but takes 2 weeks. Also consider water quality. Plastic tanks can leach chemicals if not food-grade. Ferrocement and concrete can make water alkaline if not sealed. Brick can harbour bacteria in pores. Always use a food-grade sealant. For rainwater harvesting, plastic and ferrocement are best. For borehole water with iron, concrete with a settling chamber is best. Finally, think about transport. A 10,000-litre plastic tank is 2.2m wide and 2.5m tall. It needs a truck with a crane. In rural Kenya, that costs KES 15,000 to KES 25,000. Ferrocement materials can be carried on a motorbike. That is a huge advantage. So your material selection is not just about cost. It is about logistics, skills, timeline, and water quality. Master all four, and you can serve any client in Africa.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Tank Placement, Plumbing, and Integration with Roof Catchment and Boreholes
lessons.body: A tank is only as good as its plumbing. If you cannot get water in and out efficiently, the tank is a decoration. This lesson covers placement relative to water sources, inlet and outlet design, and integration with roof catchment and boreholes. Start with roof catchment. In Africa, rainwater harvesting is a lifeline. A 100-square-metre roof in a region with 800mm annual rainfall can collect 80,000 litres per year. That is 219 litres per day on average. But rainfall is seasonal. In Kenya, the long rains come in April-May, short rains in November. You need to store enough for 3-4 dry months. For a 100-square-metre roof, you need at least 20,000 litres of storage to bridge a dry spell. The tank must be placed near the roof, but not too close. You need a first-flush diverter. This is a small pipe that collects the first 20-30 litres of rain, which contains dust, bird droppings, and leaves. Without it, your tank becomes a mud pit. A simple first-flush diverter is a 100mm PVC pipe with a ball valve. It costs KES 2,000 in Kenya, NGN 10,000 in Nigeria, GHS 100 in Ghana, ZAR 400 in South Africa. Install it before the tank inlet. The inlet should be a 100mm pipe with a mosquito screen. The tank should have an overflow pipe that directs excess water away from the foundation. In heavy rain, a 10,000-litre tank can overflow in 30 minutes. The overflow must be at least 50mm and lead to a drain or a soak pit. For boreholes, the tank is usually placed after the pump. The pump fills the tank, and gravity feeds the house. This reduces pump cycling and saves electricity. In Nigeria, where diesel generators are common, a 10,000-litre tank can reduce generator runtime by 40%. Place the tank on a tower if you need pressure. A 2-metre high tower gives 0.2 bar pressure, which is enough for a shower. A 5-metre tower gives 0.5 bar, enough for a washing machine. In Kenya, a 5-metre steel tower for a 10,000-litre tank costs KES 80,000 to KES 120,000. In Ghana, GHS 6,000 to GHS 8,000. In South Africa, ZAR 25,000 to ZAR 35,000. If you cannot afford a tower, use a pressure pump. A 0.5 HP pump costs KES 15,000 in Kenya, NGN 80,000 in Nigeria, GHS 800 in Ghana, ZAR 3,000 in South Africa. But pumps need electricity. In rural areas, gravity is more reliable. Now, plumbing details. The outlet should be at least 50mm above the tank floor to avoid sediment. Install a drain valve at the lowest point. For plastic tanks, use bulkhead fittings with rubber gaskets. Do not use silicone alone; it will fail. For ferrocement and concrete tanks, cast a 50mm PVC pipe into the wall at the bottom. Use a gate valve, not a globe valve, for full flow. For brick tanks, leave a sleeve in the wall during construction. All pipes should be UV-resistant PVC or PPR. In Africa, the sun destroys cheap pipes in 2 years. Use PN10 or PN16 pipes. For drinking water, use food-grade PVC. Never use ordinary garden hose. Also, insulate exposed pipes in hot areas. In northern Nigeria, water in a black pipe can reach 60 degrees Celsius. That is not good for drinking or for plastic tanks. Bury pipes 300mm deep or paint them white. For integration with municipal supply, install a float valve in the tank. When the tank is full, the valve shuts off the municipal water. This prevents overflow and saves money. A float valve costs KES 1,500 in Kenya, NGN 8,000 in Nigeria, GHS 80 in Ghana, ZAR 300 in South Africa. But municipal supply in many African cities is intermittent. You need a booster pump to fill the tank when pressure is low. A 0.5 HP booster pump costs the same as a pressure pump. Install a non-return valve to prevent backflow. Finally, label everything. In a commercial building, a plumber may not know which pipe is which. Use blue for potable water, green for raw water, and red for hot water. Leave a simple diagram inside the pump house. Train the client on how to clean the first-flush diverter, check the float valve, and drain sediment every 6 months. A well-plumbed tank lasts 20 years. A poorly plumbed one lasts 2. Your plumbing skills are your reputation.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Safety, Maintenance, and Business Pricing for Water Tank Construction in Africa
lessons.body: Safety is not optional. Water tank construction involves heavy materials, working at heights, and confined spaces. In Africa, we often cut corners. Do not. A fall from a 3-metre tank tower can kill. A cement burn can scar for life. A tank collapse can destroy a business. This lesson covers safety, maintenance, and how to price your work profitably. Start with personal protective equipment. You need helmets, gloves, boots, and eye protection. For mixing cement, wear a dust mask. Cement dust contains silica, which causes silicosis. In Kenya, a good dust mask costs KES 500. In Nigeria, NGN 2,500. In Ghana, GHS 25. In South Africa, ZAR 100. Buy them for your team. It is cheaper than a hospital bill. For working at heights, use a scaffold or a ladder with a second person holding it. Never stand on the tank rim. Never use a plastic tank as a ladder. For confined spaces, such as inside a concrete tank, you need ventilation. Cement curing releases carbon dioxide. A person can suffocate in minutes. Always have a second person outside. Use a blower or a fan. For electrical work, use an RCD. In Nigeria, many sites have no earth leakage. A pump can electrocute a worker. Test the pump before use. For lifting, use a crane or a pulley. A 10,000-litre plastic tank weighs 200kg empty. Two men cannot lift it safely. A crane costs KES 20,000 in Kenya, NGN 100,000 in Nigeria, GHS 1,000 in Ghana, ZAR 4,000 in South Africa. Include it in your quote. Now, maintenance. A tank needs cleaning every 6 to 12 months. Sediment builds up. Algae grows. Mosquitoes breed. For plastic tanks, you can drain and scrub with a soft brush and chlorine solution. For ferrocement and concrete, you may need to repair cracks. For brick, you must check the plaster. A maintenance contract is a business opportunity. Charge KES 5,000 per visit in Kenya, NGN 25,000 in Nigeria, GHS 250 in Ghana, ZAR 1,000 in South Africa. Do two visits per year. That is recurring income. Also sell filters and first-flush diverters. A ceramic filter costs KES 3,000 in Kenya, NGN 15,000 in Nigeria, GHS 150 in Ghana, ZAR 600 in South Africa. You can mark up 30%. Now, pricing. Many tank builders in Africa undercharge. They forget transport, labour, tools, and profit. Use this formula: Total cost = materials + labour + transport + tools + overhead + profit. Materials: calculate exactly. For a 10,000-litre ferrocement tank in Kenya, materials cost KES 50,000. Labour: 2 masons for 10 days at KES 1,500 per day = KES 30,000. Transport: KES 10,000. Tools: KES 5,000. Overhead: 10% of materials + labour = KES 8,000. Profit: 20% of total = KES 20,600. Total price = KES 123,600. That is your quote. Do not drop below 15% profit. You will go bankrupt. In Nigeria, the same tank costs NGN 350,000 in materials, NGN 200,000 labour, NGN 50,000 transport, NGN 30,000 tools, NGN 63,000 overhead, NGN 138,600 profit. Total NGN 831,600. In Ghana, GHS 3,500 materials, GHS 2,000 labour, GHS 500 transport, GHS 300 tools, GHS 630 overhead, GHS 1,386 profit. Total GHS 8,316. In South Africa, ZAR 15,000 materials, ZAR 8,000 labour, ZAR 2,000 transport, ZAR 1,500 tools, ZAR 2,650 overhead, ZAR 5,830 profit. Total ZAR 35,000. These are realistic prices. If you quote less, you are stealing from your family. Also, always ask for a 50% deposit. Buy materials with the deposit. Never use your own money. If the client refuses, walk away. There are many clients. Finally, document everything. Take photos before, during, and after. Write a simple contract. Include the tank size, material, timeline, payment schedule, and warranty. A 1-year warranty on workmanship is standard. Keep a copy. In Africa, disputes happen. A written contract protects you. Also, train the client on how to use the tank. Show them the first-flush diverter, the drain valve, and the overflow. Give them a one-page manual. This reduces callbacks. A happy client will refer you to others. That is how you build a water tank business in Africa. Safety, maintenance, and fair pricing are your pillars. Master them, and you will succeed.

quiz.q: What is the first step when sizing a water tank for a household?
quiz.explanation: Daily water demand must be known before sizing the tank.

quiz.q: Which factor most affects the required storage volume of a water tank?
options: B) Number of users and daily consumption
quiz.explanation: Storage volume depends mainly on how many people use water and how much they consume.

quiz.q: A family of 5 uses 80 liters per person per day. What is the daily demand?
quiz.explanation: 5 people multiplied by 80 liters equals 400 liters per day.

quiz.q: Why is a reserve factor added when sizing a water tank?
options: A) To account for future demand and emergencies
B) To make the tank heavier
quiz.explanation: A reserve factor covers unexpected demand and emergencies.

quiz.q: If daily demand is 500 liters and 2 days of storage are needed, what is the minimum tank size?
quiz.explanation: 500 liters per day for 2 days equals 1000 liters.

quiz.q: What does siting a water tank mean?
quiz.explanation: Siting refers to selecting the location for the tank.

quiz.q: Which location is generally best for a water tank?
options: B) On firm, level ground near the point of use
C) Directly over a septic tank
quiz.explanation: Firm level ground near use reduces pumping and structural risks.

quiz.q: Why should a water tank be placed close to the point of use?
options: A) To reduce pipe length and friction losses
B) To make it look better
quiz.explanation: Shorter pipes reduce friction losses and material costs.

quiz.q: What is a key reason to avoid siting a tank downhill from a latrine?
options: B) Risk of contamination from runoff
quiz.explanation: Runoff from a latrine can contaminate a downhill tank.

quiz.q: Which soil condition is unsuitable for a heavy water tank?
quiz.explanation: Soft expansive clay can settle and crack the tank.

quiz.q: What should be done before placing a tank on soil?
options: A) Compact and level the ground
quiz.explanation: Compacting and leveling prevents uneven settlement.

quiz.q: Why is a concrete base often recommended under a water tank?
options: A) To spread the load and prevent settling
B) To make the tank colorful
quiz.explanation: A base spreads the tank load over a larger area.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a tank stand?
options: A) To raise the tank for gravity flow
quiz.explanation: Elevation allows gravity to provide water pressure.

quiz.q: How much height is needed for gravity flow to a tap?
options: B) At least about 1 meter above the tap
quiz.explanation: About 1 meter of head gives usable gravity pressure.

quiz.q: What is the relationship between tank height and water pressure?
options: A) Higher tank gives higher pressure
B) Higher tank gives lower pressure
C) Height does not affect pressure
D) Pressure depends only on color
quiz.explanation: Pressure increases with the height of the water column.

quiz.q: Which factor is important when siting a tank in a windy area?
quiz.explanation: Wind can overturn or damage an unsecured tank.

quiz.q: Why should a tank be sited away from tree roots?
options: A) Roots can crack the base and tank
quiz.explanation: Growing roots can damage foundations and tank walls.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of siting a tank in direct sunlight in hot climates?
quiz.explanation: Sunlight warms water and promotes algae and evaporation.

quiz.q: Which tank material is most suitable for underground siting?
quiz.explanation: Reinforced concrete resists soil pressure and moisture.

quiz.q: What is the minimum recommended distance from a tank to a septic tank?
quiz.explanation: A separation of at least 15 meters reduces contamination risk.

quiz.q: What does peak demand mean in tank sizing?
options: A) Highest water use in a short period
quiz.explanation: Peak demand is the maximum usage over a short time.

quiz.q: Why is fire storage sometimes included in tank sizing?
options: A) To provide water for firefighting
quiz.explanation: Fire storage ensures water is available during a fire.

quiz.q: What is the effect of undersizing a water tank?
quiz.explanation: An undersized tank cannot meet demand and causes shortages.

quiz.q: What is the effect of oversizing a water tank?
options: A) Higher cost and possible stagnation
quiz.explanation: Oversized tanks cost more and water may stagnate.

quiz.q: Which unit is commonly used for household tank capacity?
quiz.explanation: Tank capacity is usually measured in liters.

quiz.q: How many liters are in one cubic meter?
quiz.explanation: One cubic meter equals 1000 liters.

quiz.q: What is the volume of a tank 2 m long, 1 m wide, and 1 m high?
quiz.explanation: Volume equals length times width times height, so 2 x 1 x 1 equals 2 cubic meters.

quiz.q: Why should a tank site allow easy access for maintenance?
options: A) To clean, inspect, and repair the tank
quiz.explanation: Access is needed for cleaning, inspection, and repairs.

quiz.q: What should be considered about the water source when siting a tank?
options: A) Distance and elevation from the source
quiz.explanation: Distance and elevation affect pumping and pipe design.

quiz.q: Which is a sign of a poorly sited water tank?
quiz.explanation: Settlement from poor siting often causes cracks.
